strengths: The paper derives a clean and well-motivated self-consistency property (Theorem 2.1) of the diffusion bridge control via the Jacobian process, and a characterization result (Theorem 3.1) that justifies a fixed-point-style training objective. The connection to the adjoint matching / SOCM literature (Appendix B.5) is insightful and places the work in context.

The proposed algorithm avoids backpropagation through simulated trajectories, giving a concrete scalability advantage over the most comparable method (NGDB): ~230s vs ~800s for 5000 steps on the OU bridge, with competitive or better KL to the ground truth (Figures 3a-c, Table 1).

The paper is unusually thorough in diagnosing practical failure modes: Jacobian explosion is analysed (Appendix B.4), and the generalised self-consistency property with auxiliary drift (Theorems B.1, B.2) is both theoretically grounded and empirically shown to be essential on the double-well and Müller-Brown examples (Figure 9, Table 2).

Experimental evaluation covers five benchmark settings (OU, CIR, double-well, cell diffusion, Müller-Brown), four baselines, and useful ablations (α-schedules in Table 3, STL adjustments in Table 4, dimension and parameter sensitivity), with mean±std over 5 runs and explicit KL metrics against ground truth where available.

Limitations are discussed honestly (ellipticity requirement, need to simulate the current process during training), implementation details and baseline code licenses are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Originality is somewhat incremental. The authors themselves acknowledge (Appendix A) that the self-consistency property can be derived from the Malliavin calculus framework of Pidstrigach et al. (2025), and the fixed-point loss design follows Domingo-Enrich et al. (2024, 2025). The main novelty is the adaptation to the singular diffusion-bridge setting plus the generalised (b̃) variant, which is useful but a modest delta.

There is no convergence theory for the proposed iterative 'self-play' scheme. Theorems 2.1/3.1 only characterise the fixed point; whether the fixed-point iteration is stable, and under what conditions it converges, is left unaddressed despite empirical evidence that training can be unstable (e.g., b̃ = 0 failing on Müller-Brown, loss clipping needed).

The uniqueness result (Theorem 3.1 / D.2) leans on well-known reciprocal-class results, and the (iii)⇔(iv) direction invokes uniqueness of solutions to a parabolic PDE for the vorticity 'under standard regularity assumptions' citing Pazy (2012) without verifying those assumptions for the bridge control, which is singular at the terminal time; the rigour here is not airtight.

The bridging property is enforced by 'jumping directly to xT' in the final discretisation step, which introduces a discretisation bias near the singular terminal time; the paper does not quantify how this bias scales with δt, and KL values are truncated near T in the CIR experiment to avoid numerical issues.

Experimental scale is limited to low-dimensional synthetic problems (d ≤ 30); the motivating claim of applicability to rare events and scientific applications is supported only qualitatively (Figures 4, 5, 7, 8). No high-dimensional or real-data evaluation is provided, and the paper does not claim to beat NGDB, only to match it at lower cost.
Reproducibility of the proposed method itself is incomplete: Appendix E lists only codebases of the baselines; no link to the authors' own implementation or release is provided.

strengths: The paper is well written and clearly structured, with an intuitive motivating figure (Figure 1) and a clean separation between the necessary self-consistency property and the additional gradient-form/bridging conditions needed for sufficiency.

The characterization result (Theorem 3.1 / Theorem D.2), showing that the diffusion bridge is the unique gradient-form bridge-preserving control satisfying self-consistency, provides genuine theoretical support for the proposed loss family, and the connections drawn in Appendix B.5 to adjoint matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) and SOCM are insightful.

The practical selling point is real and quantified: removing backpropagation through simulated trajectories yields roughly a 3.5x speed-up over NGDB (230s vs 800s for 5000 OU steps) with competitive KL values, and this is a meaningful scalability advantage.

The experimental section is reasonably thorough for its scope: quantitative KL metrics against closed-form ground truth (OU, CIR, double-well), ablations over α-schedules and STL adjustments (Tables 3, 4), and an honest accounting of where the method fails without the generalised auxiliary-drift trick (Müller-Brown, Figure 9).

Reproducibility treatment is good: architectures, hyperparameters, learning rates, hardware, and baseline codebase links are all provided, and the limitations (ellipticity requirement, reliance on simulating the current process) are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: Originality is limited: the authors themselves concede (Appendix A) that the core self-consistency property 'can also be derived from the Malliavin calculus framework of Pidstrigach et al. (2025)', and the fixed-point/self-play regression scheme closely mirrors adjoint matching and SOCM (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2024, 2025). The contribution is essentially a transfer of known matching-loss machinery to the bridge setting plus the gradient-form parameterisation trick, which weakens the case for a main-track paper.

Theorem 3.1 is stated imprecisely for the continuous-time setting. Controlled processes of the form (3) do not 'terminate at xT' almost surely unless the control is singular (as it is for the true bridge, growing like 1/(T-t)); in practice the bridging property is enforced only by a discrete-time jump to xT in the final step, so the uniqueness claim underpinning the method's justification is looser than presented. The regularity assumptions behind the vorticity argument (Equation 69, uniqueness via Pazy 2012) are not verified near the terminal time where the control is singular.

There is no convergence or error analysis for the training procedure. The fixed-point loss has two coupled dependencies on u (through values and through trajectories), and the paper offers no theoretical or empirical study of when this self-play iteration converges to u* rather than an unstable fixed point; instead, success relies on a collection of empirical heuristics (b̃ = −b, loss clipping at 1e4, choice among three α-schedules).

The headline experimental evidence is modest in scale and partly unfavourable. Benchmarks are low-dimensional (d ≤ 30) synthetic potentials; NGDB outperforms the proposed method in the rare and multimodal cell-diffusion settings and has lower variance in the harder Müller-Brown experiment, so the honest claim is 'comparable at lower cost', which is an incremental advance. The KL(Pθ‖P) surrogate metric used where ground truth is unavailable is acknowledged by the authors to be unreliable (the asterisked SDB result), further weakening the quantitative case.

The method as presented in the main text fails on the flagship harder experiment: the standard algorithm (b̃ = 0) 'generally failed to learn the correct dynamics' on Müller-Brown, and only the generalised variant relegated to Appendix B.4/Algorithm 2 works. This means the effective method is more complicated than the main-text presentation suggests, and the choice of b̃ introduces an additional design decision without principled guidance.

Several baseline comparisons are inherently handicapped (SDB and FB learn from unconditioned dynamics and predictably fail for rare events, as the authors note), which inflates the apparent strength of the empirical contribution; the only genuinely competitive comparison is a single baseline (NGDB), tuned with the authors' own conservative architecture choice.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: the paper derives a self-consistency property of the optimal bridge control (Theorem 2.1) in terms of the Jacobian process, and combines it with a characterisation result (Theorem 3.1) to obtain a fixed-point-style training objective that avoids backpropagation through simulated trajectories. The proofs in Appendix D are worked out in reasonable detail, including the singular bridge case F = δ_{x_T}, the generalised Girsanov-based property (Theorem B.1/B.2), and the sticking-the-landing adjustments.

The empirical evaluation is appropriately targeted at the claimed use case: rare-event conditioning where unconditioned-training methods (SDB, FB) fail, and comparison against NGDB, the strongest online-learning baseline. Results on OU, CIR, double-well, cell diffusion, and Müller-Brown are reported with ground-truth KL where available and multiple seeds (mean±std over 5 runs).

The ablations are unusually thorough: α-schedules (next-step/average/endpoint), STL adjustments, and the auxiliary-drift generalisation b̃ = −b are each examined, and the paper is honest about when its own standard variant fails (e.g. Müller-Brown with b̃ = 0) and explains why via Jacobian growth.

The claimed speed-up (no backprop through trajectories) is substantiated with concrete timings (~230s vs ~800s for 5000 OU training steps), and reproducibility is addressed via architecture details, hyperparameters, and links to baseline codebases.

The discussion of connections to stochastic optimal control (adjoint matching, SOCM) in Appendix B.5 positions the contribution well within the literature and shows the framework subsumes/interrupts known objectives.
weaknesses: No convergence theory for the practical algorithm. The theoretical characterisation (Theorem 3.1) concerns the exact fixed point, but there is no analysis of the self-play/fixed-point optimisation scheme: no stability, convergence, or bias analysis of the stopgrad regression (9), nor conditions under which iterating it reaches the diffusion bridge. Given the paper's own observation that training can be unstable (loss clipping at 1e4, need for b̃ = −b, α-schedule sensitivity), this gap between characterisation and algorithm is material.

The uniqueness result (Theorem 3.1/D.2) leans on PDE uniqueness 'under standard regularity assumptions' (citing Pazy) which is stated informally; the singular case F = δ_{x_T} is handled by approximation and a limiting argument that is sketched rather than rigorously justified.

Experimental scale is modest: all benchmarks are low-dimensional (d ≤ 2-30 synthetic OU) with short horizons. There is no evidence on the problems that motivate the method most (e.g. realistic molecular systems), and the abstract's framing around rare events in the sciences is supported mainly by synthetic rare-event variants.

Performance is comparable rather than superior: the headline result is matching NGDB at lower cost, and in the rare/multimodal cell-diffusion settings NGDB actually performs slightly better. The practical advantage rests substantially on the wall-clock speed-up, which is reported for only one experiment.

The self-consistency property is acknowledged (Appendix A) to be derivable from the Malliavin calculus framework of Pidstrigach et al. (2025); the novelty is therefore mainly in the fixed-point/online loss construction and its sufficiency characterisation (Theorem 3.1), which narrows the conceptual contribution somewhat.

Several practical choices (α-schedule, b̃, STL, loss clipping) require case-by-case tuning per experiment, and the paper does not provide guidance general enough to guarantee out-of-the-box reliability on new problems.
